title: A Terrible Truth: The Tonkawa Massacre of 1862
author: Joseph Connole
publisher: Chronicles of Oklahoma, 97(4), Winter 2019–2020, pp. 450–467; Oklahoma Historical Society / Gateway to Oklahoma History, UNT Libraries
annotation: An 18-page article in the Oklahoma Historical Society’s scholarly journal. Connole compares explanations for the 1862 attack and argues that long-running political alliances and failures of federal and Confederate protection shaped the Tonkawa’s vulnerability. This is the author’s secondary interpretation, not a Tonkawa-authored account or a settled consensus; his own opening discussion says the instigators and immediate reasons remain unclear.
contentReviewScope: Complete article body, printed pp. 450–465, and selected endnotes pp. 466–467 inspected from the UNT/Oklahoma Historical Society digital copy. The author relies on cited historical scholarship and government reports; most cited underlying records were not independently re-read in this pass. The article notes one known first-hand account of the Fort Cobb attack. Its casualty estimate and causal interpretation remain attributed. The map and archival photograph were not separately inspected.

title: Historia de la tribu kikapú y de su problemática
publisher: Elisabeth A. Mager Hois; Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (CISAN, Instituto de Investigaciones Antropológicas, FES Acatlán)
annotation: This 2010 Spanish-language book chapter surveys Kickapoo histories from the Great Lakes to Coahuila and Texas and discusses the formation of the Texas community, cross-border relations, land, federal recognition, and the Lucky Eagle casino context. It is a scholarly synthesis by one author drawing on earlier publications and field interviews with Kickapoo and Múzquiz residents (1996–2002); its interpretations are not a community-authored consensus. The chapter itself notes contradictory dates and figures in cited works, including the 1873 El Remolino attack and land-area totals. Read those passages as attributed historical claims rather than settled facts. The repository lists open access and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; only a link is reproduced here.
contentReviewScope: Full 13-page chapter read (printed pages 101–113), including historical narrative, El Nacimiento and Texas sections, source notes, and references.
accessNotes: Open-access PDF through UNAM repository; Spanish language; repository metadata lists CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

title: Ethnic Consciousness in Cultural Survival: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians and the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas
publisher: Elisabeth A. Mager; translation by Heather Dashner Monk; American Indian Culture and Research Journal / eScholarship, University of California
annotation: This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. Mager identifies documentary research, participant observation, and interviews as methods and cites interviews conducted from 1995 to 2015, along with the Texas Tribe’s 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. Selected passages discuss land acquisition and economic history; the author’s theory of “ethnic consciousness,” causal claims, and generalizations remain her interpretation, not a community consensus. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.
contentReviewScope: Read article metadata and research-method statement (printed pp.47–48), Kickapoo-focused land and Texas economic-history passages (printed pp.61–63), and the corresponding cited notes on printed p.71. The comparative sections about Morongo and detailed ceremonial/cultural descriptions were not used. Claims are attributed to the author and the dates/interview sources stated in her notes.
accessNotes: Full article publicly available from eScholarship; its record lists a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial license. The atlas links to the article and does not reproduce its text or images.

title: No-ko-aht’s Talk: A Kickapoo Chief’s Account of a Tribal Journey from Kansas to Mexico and Return in the Sixties
publisher: George A. Root, editor; Kansas Historical Society; account recorded by Franklin G. Adams
annotation: The article prints a May 31, 1867 account attributed to Kickapoo leader No-ko-aht and recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams. No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.
publicationDate: Interview recorded May 31, 1867; edited/published February 1932, Kansas Historical Quarterly 1(2), pp. 153–159
contentReviewScope: Full transcribed article and footnotes read, pp.153–159. Inspected the editor’s account and the attributed No-ko-aht statement; no independent corroboration of every event, date, casualty number, or quotation was established.
accessNotes: Public transcription hosted by Kansas Historical Society; source page states digitized with permission. Historical spellings, editorial framing, and one illegible passage are retained as source limitations.

title: Early History of the Creek Indians and Their Neighbors: The Abihka
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology
author: John R. Swanton
annotation: Bulletin 73 (1922), printed pp. 251–254; inspected the Abihka text and a public-domain scan of pp. 252–254. Compiles earlier records and named narrators; useful for conflicting etymologies and Abihkutci distinctions. Dated interpretations and historical descriptions need comparison with community accounts. Link opens the Smithsonian record and full PDF.

title: Source Material on the History and Ethnology of the Caddo Indians
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 132; full-text transcription hosted by the Louisiana Anthology
author: John R. Swanton
annotation: 1942 sourcebook. Inspected selected Adai passages on printed pp. 13–15, 21–23, 75, and 84–85. Swanton compares discrepant population estimates, reports Caddo recollections, and warns that a later village called Adaise cannot securely be identified as Indigenous. Its historical synthesis and quoted records require source-specific reading. His assertion that Adai were entirely merged with other Caddo is a dated author's conclusion, not a verdict on today's communities or their identities.

title: A Dictionary of the Biloxi and Ofo Languages, Accompanied with Thirty-one Biloxi Texts and Numerous Biloxi Phrases
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 47
annotation: The foundational 1912 collection preserves Biloxi texts and vocabulary alongside a distinct Ofo dictionary. Reviewed the contents and Biloxi introduction, pp. 1–4, through the public-domain Wikisource transcription because the institutional PDF could not be fetched. The introduction explains editorial rearrangement and notation; this is not a full review of all texts.

title: MS 2424 Attacapa-English dictionary
author: John R. Swanton and Delilah Morse; archival collection record
type: Archival finding aid / supporting primary-source locator
annotation: The Smithsonian finding aid identifies an archival card collection with Swanton and Delilah Morse, dates, holdings, and a note separating Eastern-dialect material from Akokisa vocabulary attributed to an earlier publication. The cards and slips themselves were not inspected, so this is a locator and does not contribute to the substantive count.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible catalogue record and its local note. The archival collection itself was not opened; access and reproduction conditions were not verified.

title: Teaching Traditions: Public Programming at the Alutiiq Museum
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of the American Indian, in Living Homes for Cultural Expression
author: Amy F. Steffian; volume edited by Karen Coody Cooper and Nicolasa I. Sandoval
annotation: A substantial museum practitioner's account of community archaeology, heritage organizing and choices about public education. It records disagreements and an Alutiiq-first mission rather than presenting revival as an outside discovery. Program examples and institutional circumstances are dated to this 2006 chapter.
contentReviewScope: Selected actual chapter passages: opening pages 27–28; Programs Create the Museum, pages 32–33; A Philosophy for Programming, pages 34–35; and public-education examples, pages 36–37. Title/copyright pages checked. Not a full-volume review.

title: Notes on the History and Material Culture of the Tonkawa Indians
publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 2(5)
author: William K. Jones
annotation: Jones places a historical sketch alongside a study of objects collected by U.S. Army surgeon Henry McElderry at Fort Griffin in 1868. The work is valuable for its named documents and the history of the collection, but it reflects a 1969 museum and ethnological framework and relies on older colonial and scholarly accounts. Its proposed archaeological links and broad identity/language classifications are uncertain or dated and are not treated as settled evidence. Object descriptions and images are not reproduced here.
contentReviewScope: Read the title/contents, introduction, selected historical-sketch pages (printed pp. 65–71), the conclusion section (printed p. 77), and selected bibliography/context passages. The full object catalogue on printed pp. 74–76 was not reviewed; maps listed by the work were not inspected as images.

title: The Classification and Distribution of the Pit River Indian Tribes of California
author: C. Hart Merriam
annotation: Published December 31, 1926, pp. 1–52. Read printed pp. 1–5, 12–14, 24–26, and selected name entries on pp. 41–47 in the full scan. Merriam acknowledges named Indigenous contributors and records variable names and contrasting environments. His narrower Fall River use of A-choo-mah-we and period classification require context; the map and taxonomy do not establish present jurisdiction or modern band membership. His salvage-era assumptions should not be repeated as statements about contemporary people.

title: Modern Square Grounds of the Creek Indians
author: John R. Swanton
annotation: Published November 11, 1931. Read introduction pp. 1–4 and Abihka pp. 13–15, including the author’s explanation of changed information. Documents Abihka/Talladega near Henryetta through dated fieldwork. This historical publication includes culturally sensitive ceremonial detail; its availability does not authorize reproducing practices or assuming current arrangements.

title: MS 2516: Alsea and Lower Umpqua texts and notes
annotation: Finding aid distinguishes Alsea notebooks from a Lower Umpqua grammatical index and records corrections to notebook authorship. This describes holdings and research routes; it does not turn every linked manuscript into an inspected work.
contentReviewScope: Actual finding-aid summary and scope/content notes read. No linked manuscript images or recordings inspected. Supporting reference outside the substantive target.

annotation: The Band's public self-account and overlapping mission page are grouped once. They contribute its own perspective, without independently proving every historical claim, current program or legal status. Application, incorporation and community identity remain distinct.

author: Tāp Pīlam Coahuiltecan Nation
publicationDate: Undated community timeline; dates within page are attributed there
annotation: The Nation’s own public timeline is a first-party account of Tāp Pīlam history and community continuity. Its sweeping chronology and deep-time claims are presented as the Nation’s account, not as independently verified claims about every South Texas people. Read alongside group-specific historical research.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible History timeline, including its dated periods, mission-era entries and contemporary organizational chronology. The linked image and underlying archival or archaeological evidence were not independently examined.

author: Tāp Pīlam Coahuiltecan Nation
annotation: A community site index linking public resolutions and proclamations. It is useful as a route to primary documents, not as a substantive historical work. The page also includes placeholder text and unverified membership figures; those are not used.
contentReviewScope: Inspected the full visible listing and linked document labels. The page’s placeholder copy and membership figures were excluded; the linked instruments are not counted as separately inspected here.

title: La Junta Reconsidered
author: Jefferson Morgenthaler and collaborators; author byline not shown on page
publicationDate: Undated web exhibit; page references Morgenthaler’s 2007 book
annotation: A separate educational synthesis about La Junta’s archaeology and changing interpretations. It explains why Jumano cannot simply stand for everyone who lived at or visited the confluence, and summarizes Kelley, Kenmotsu, and Morgenthaler models. Its statements about the disappearance of Native groups are attributed historical interpretations, not proof that descendant communities no longer exist.
contentReviewScope: The full visible La Junta Reconsidered page was read, including its treatment of competing models and research limits. Cited books, archival material, and underlying archaeological data were not independently inspected.

title: Who Were the Jumano? / Jumano-Spanish Relations
author: Nancy A. Kenmotsu; exhibit editor Steve Black
publicationDate: Undated web exhibit; credits cite adaptation from Kenmotsu’s 1994 dissertation and 2001 article
annotation: An educational exhibit that synthesizes Spanish accounts of trade, diplomacy, missions, and conflict. Its author explicitly adopts the interpretation that Jumano was a distinct nation. The later statement that Jumano culture was gone and the treatment of biological ‘blood’ are dated outsider interpretations that conflict with contemporary community accounts and should not be presented as established fact.
contentReviewScope: Both substantive Jumano modules and the credits page were read. The exhibit’s embedded translations and secondary figures were inspected as presented; cited books, dissertation, article, archives, and maps were not independently reviewed.

title: Los Adaes — Cultural Worlds, archival research, and legacy
publisher: Texas Beyond History · Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
author: Hiram F. Gregory, George Avery, Francis X. Galán, Steve Black, and contributors including Mariah F. Wade
annotation: Read Cultural Worlds, Los Adaes Archival Research, Legacy, and the contributor credits. The exhibit distinguishes Adai communities from the colonial establishment and discusses Indigenous-made pottery, trade, and later heritage. Its contributors include an Adai specialist and acknowledge Chief Rufus Davis’s assistance. Some language about disappearance and colonial cultural hierarchies is dated; do not adopt it as a verdict on living identity. The linked exhibit sections count as one resource, not four.

title: Early Encounters, 1535–1714 (La Junta de los Ríos exhibit)
publisher: Texas Beyond History / Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
author: William A. (Andy) Cloud, Steve Black, and Jennifer Piehl; additional writing by Carly Whelan and David Hill
annotation: A detailed exhibit chapter that distinguishes settled La Junta communities from Jumano visitors and traders, and discusses translation problems, Spanish slave raids, diplomacy, and Juan Sabeata. Its statements are an educational synthesis of secondary literature and translated colonial accounts; the underlying manuscripts and archaeology are not independently verified here. The page itself cautions that historic group names and localities can be difficult to match.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible chapter, map and illustration captions, and author/credit material were read. Cited translations and archaeological studies were not independently inspected. Historic maps embedded in the exhibit were not inspected as map objects or reviewed for reuse; no map was added to the Atlas.

title: Native Peoples in a Spanish World — Mission Espíritu Santo
author: Texas Beyond History exhibit contributors
publisher: Texas Beyond History, University of Texas at Austin and Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
annotation: A focused case study of people associated with three locations of Mission Espíritu Santo, especially Aranama, Tamiques and Manos de Prieta. The exhibit records disagreement over possible Aranama/Mariame equivalence and notes sparse, ambiguous Spanish documentation. Its statements concern this mission setting, not every group placed under the broader label.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible Native Peoples page and its mission-specific discussion. Linked mission records and the exhibit’s archaeological sources were not independently opened.

title: Who Were the “Coahuiltecans”?
author: Texas Beyond History exhibit contributors; source credits identify the underlying researchers
publisher: Texas Beyond History, University of Texas at Austin and Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
annotation: An educational synthesis presenting Coahuiltecan as a geographic catch-all for diverse South Texas and northeastern Mexico peoples. It names Payaya, Pacuache and Mariames and describes seasonal movement, language diversity and overlapping relationships. Its deep-time continuity inference and other reconstructions are the exhibit authors’ interpretations, not demonstrated genealogies for every named people.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete substantive exhibit page, its historical and foodways passages, the ending and credits/source links. Embedded primary quotations were read as presented; cited works and archival records were not opened independently.

title: First Villagers — La Junta de los Ríos exhibit — Texas Beyond History
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Center for Big Bend Studies, Sul Ross State University
author: William A. Cloud, Steve Black and Jennifer Piehl; additional contributors named in the credits
annotation: This exhibit describes archaeological evidence for early La Junta villages, trade, subsistence and competing models of population continuity. The authors distinguish archaeological phases from the later Spanish-recorded communities and describe the identification of early villagers as unknown. It gives valuable context for the region, but does not identify an archaeological phase as Jumano. Interpretive disagreement is stated in the exhibit and should remain attributed.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible “First Villagers” article, its image captions/credits and the full exhibit credits/source page (lines 23–64). The cited archaeological reports and underlying collections were not independently read; no illustration is reproduced.

title: Reviving a Lost Tradition
publisher: Texas Beyond History; interview within the Created in Clay exhibit
annotation: Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn describes her own process of learning and reviving pottery practice and reflects on removals and boarding schools. This is a named person’s first-person account, not a claim that one maker speaks for all Caddo people.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible interview page and credited contextual material were read. The profile attributes its reflections to Redcorn and does not reproduce restricted or unpublished material.

title: Caddo Homeland
publisher: Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter
annotation: Cecile Elkins Carter, an enrolled Caddo historian, presents a Caddo-centered synthesis using oral history, archival records, and historical group names. The page distinguishes broad Caddo use from the narrower historical Cadohadacho label; these are attributed historical interpretations rather than a universal current naming rule.
contentReviewScope: The full visible page and the separate credits page were read. Its account is Carter’s researched and written synthesis; underlying cited archives and all referenced books were not independently reviewed.

title: Twenty Years Without a Home, 1836–1859
publisher: Texas Beyond History; researched and written by Cecile Elkins Carter
annotation: This page follows displacement and movement among Louisiana, Texas, the Brazos area, and Indian Territory using archival records and named Caddo testimony. Testimony from Fallis Elkins (1973) and Sadie Bedoka Weller (1968) is identified by speaker and date; it is situated family memory, not a generic or interchangeable Caddo story.
contentReviewScope: The full visible page, narrative, map caption, archival references, and attributed oral-history excerpts were read. The complete recordings and all referenced primary records were not inspected.

title: Caddo Ancestors: Uncovering Early Caddo History
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
annotation: This exhibit overview explains its archaeological and historical questions, the long chronology it covers, and the uncertainty in reconstructing pre-written history. Its linked chapters offer a deeper reading path; only the overview was inspected for this review.
contentReviewScope: The full visible overview and chapter descriptions were inspected; individual linked chapter pages were not read and are not claimed as inspected.

title: Caddo Homeland: the Land and its Resources
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
annotation: A detailed exhibit places Caddo communities within river systems and landscapes while explaining that territorial reach changed through time. Its map and text also distinguish a broad northern Arkansas Basin area where identity and archaeological classification are debated.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible homeland page, its map caption, geographic description, and discussion of changing extent and disputed northern affiliation were read. The map is a scholarly exhibit, not a legal or present-day territorial boundary.

title: Caddo Timeline
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
annotation: A chronological overview explains that archaeological timelines are useful scholarly tools but cannot capture most individual experiences or all events. It identifies the need to compare archaeology with oral, written, linguistic, and community evidence.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible timeline page and its methodological caveats, chronology, captions, and cited source leads were read. Cited books and records were not independently inspected unless separately listed.

title: Created in Clay: the Caddo Pottery Tradition
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
annotation: This exhibit explains the archaeological importance of Caddo pottery and directs readers to a separate account of contemporary Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn’s practice. The archaeological framing and present-day artistic work are connected but should not be collapsed into a claim that cultural practices are unchanged.
contentReviewScope: The full visible exhibit introduction and its described pottery galleries and linked sections were read. Gallery images and the separate pages are not counted as independently inspected here.

title: Learning About the Caddo Past
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory and partners
annotation: This methods essay describes the strengths and limitations of oral history, archaeology, linguistics, ethnography, and European accounts. It directly cautions that missionary and explorer records can reflect the authors’ motives and prejudices, a useful guide for interpreting older documentary sources.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible essay, named source traditions, image captions, and bibliography leads were inspected. The books and archival documents it describes remain separate leads unless listed as inspected.

title: Coastal Prairies and Marshes: Native Peoples of the Texas Coast
publisher: Texas Beyond History; Texas Archeological Research Laboratory, The University of Texas at Austin
annotation: An archaeologist-authored public teaching exhibit places Karankawa communities within a wider Texas coastal region and links settlement, material evidence and seasonal mobility. It was published in 2009 and uses a period “gone forever” framing in its regional introduction; that framing does not establish the absence of living descendants and is balanced with later community sources.
contentReviewScope: The complete Native Peoples overview, Karankawa section, credits and bibliography were read. Linked site reports and cited books were not independently inspected; the page’s regional map is an explanatory scholarly illustration, not a present-day territorial boundary.

title: Part-time Farmers: Patarabueyes of La Junta — Texas Beyond History
publisher: Texas Beyond History; University of Texas at Austin
author: Nancy A. Kenmotsu
annotation: This Trans-Pecos exhibit discusses Patarabueye villages and named communities at La Junta, using Spanish records and archaeological context. It states that Jumano groups were friendly with La Junta peoples but less often found there. The page is useful for keeping neighboring and allied peoples distinct; it does not make the Patarabueyes and Jumano interchangeable or establish one identity for all La Junta villages. Its historical interpretations are the author’s synthesis of colonial records and cited scholarship.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible “Part-time Farmers: Patarabueyes of La Junta” page and its credits/source page (including named author and bibliography). The linked scholarship and archival documents were not independently reviewed; illustrations and photographs were not inspected as cultural evidence.

title: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma Research Report — TxDOT Tribal Histories
author: Texas Department of Transportation; individual report author not identified in the inspected text
annotation: This 30-page chronological research report compiles scholarship and records for Texas transportation planning and public education. TxDOT describes its broader Tribal Histories project as collaborative with participating Tribes, but the Tonkawa report itself does not identify a specific Tribal reviewer or approval; it is therefore treated as a government synthesis, not as a Tonkawa-authored account. Its reconstructions of early bands, locations, and 1862 casualty totals remain attributed to the report and cited literature.
contentReviewScope: Read the report introduction and selected chronology: PDF pages 3–10, 15–29, including bibliography entries at pages 29–30. Pages 11–14 and most bibliography entries were not reviewed. Figures/maps were not visually inspected and are not used as map evidence.

title: TxDOT Tribal Histories: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Research Report
author: TxDOT Tribal Histories Project research team, developed in consultation with Ysleta del Sur Pueblo’s Department of Cultural Preservation
annotation: A 2021 TxDOT research report prepared for transportation planning and public education. Its introduction says the source set was recommended and approved by Ysleta del Sur Pueblo’s Director of Cultural Preservation, who also commented on the draft. The report combines historical scholarship, archival material, community publications, oral history and GIS work. It is a collaboratively informed government research synthesis, not a Pueblo-authored monograph; colonial-era accounts and interpretations remain attributed to the sources it cites. This profile uses public historical context and omits location-level details identified as culturally sensitive for future planning.
contentReviewScope: PDF text was extracted and substantive pages 3–4, 21–22, 28–35 and the bibliography on 37–40 were read for project method, movement/settlement framing, land-tenure history, military service and federal recognition. Page 36’s culturally sensitive planning section and its location-level information were deliberately excluded from profile synthesis. Appendices/GIS data, maps and photographs were not independently inspected; no coordinates or sensitive locations were used.

title: Tribal Histories: Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana Research Report
publisher: Texas Department of Transportation, Tribal Histories Project
author: No individual author identified in inspected title/introduction; Louisiana tribal collaboration explicitly acknowledged
annotation: A substantial geographic history was developed with Louisiana tribal heritage staff using recommended and approved sources. It examines Coushatta presence in Texas, rather than equating a government’s present address with its whole history. Maps and precise sites are not reused.
contentReviewScope: Actual 24-page PDF: title/contents, introduction and selected history on 3–7, village/trail discussion 9–12 and settlement/reservation discussion 16–17. Not a complete report, underlying-reference, GIS or rights review.

title: Caddo Mounds History
annotation: A site history summarizes the settlement and ceremonial center at Caddo Mounds and later Hasinai and Caddo movement. Its account is useful for this particular site and institutional chronology, not a complete history of the Caddo people.
contentReviewScope: The full visible history article and its listed chronology were read. Interpretations of why the center was vacated remain attributed to the site’s archaeological account.

title: History Programs public packet: Karankawa marker-text request
annotation: Selected pages preserve a dated public review of a request to revise a Karankawa historical marker, including community-submitted material and competing procedural recommendations. A committee packet is not a complete meeting transcript or a current statement of marker wording.
contentReviewScope: Only PDF pages 43–47 concerning the Karankawa Campsite marker item were inspected. The packet contains submitted assertions and proposed motions; no final vote or current marker status is inferred from these selected pages.
sourceKind: Selected pages of government meeting record

title: History Programs quarterly packet: proposed Karankawa marker text
annotation: A later Texas Historical Commission quarterly packet contains a proposed Karankawa marker text, but it largely repeats one institutional narrative and predates a reported 2026 marker replacement. Kept as a dated comparison, not current marker text or an independent substantive history.
contentReviewScope: Selected Karankawa marker-text pages in the November 2025 packet were inspected. The complete report was not read, and no final/current marker status is inferred from this source.

title: The History of the Alabama-Coushatta and Their Role in the Texas Revolution
annotation: A state historical agency’s 2026 educational article recounts Alabama-Coushatta histories and their role in the Texas Revolution, drawing on named secondary books, a state resolution, the 1836 treaty record and an attributed statement by Chief Colita. It represents a modern state-commemoration frame. Claims are attributed to the article and its cited works; its interpretive summary is not treated as community-authored history or independent corroboration.
contentReviewScope: Complete article body, dated February 24, 2026, read, including its named sources and displayed image captions. The underlying cited books, resolution, original manuscript and image rights were not separately reviewed. Only the article’s cautious historical context is used.

title: Plan Your Visit to Caddo Mounds
publisher: Texas Historical Commission and Caddo Nation of Oklahoma
annotation: The state’s current visitor page documents the 2024 reopening and says the site is held in trust and actively managed by the Texas Historical Commission and Caddo Nation. This is a site-management and visitor account, not a general statement about Caddo government or land title elsewhere.
contentReviewScope: The page sections on reopening, site management, public interpretation, and visits were read. Admission and schedule details are not reproduced because they can change.

title: Caddo Voices interactive exhibit
publisher: Texas Historical Commission, in collaboration with Caddo citizens
annotation: This public exhibit says it was designed with Caddo citizens and features Caddo artist Chase Kahwinhut Earles. It connects selected knowledge about Caddo Mounds, the High Temple Mound, gardens, the grass house, and present gatherings; it is one collaborative interpretation, not a statement by every Caddo citizen.
contentReviewScope: The visible exhibit text and chapters for High Temple Mound, prairie/garden, grass house, Low Platform Mound, and burial mound were inspected. Embedded external material and any cultural knowledge outside the public exhibit were not accessed.

title: Treaty between Texas and the Cherokee Indians, February 23, 1836 (transcribed in Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. I)
author: Republic of Texas commissioners and Cherokee representatives; edited by Dorman H. Winfrey and James M. Day
publisher: Texas History Trust, Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest
annotation: The printed treaty text lists Alabama and Coushatta among groups it calls Cherokee “associate Bands” and proposes that the named bands form one community within specified bounds. This is a Republic of Texas diplomatic document in colonial/state language, mediated through a later edited transcription. Its text does not establish that the proposed agreement was ratified, implemented, or accepted as a lasting boundary by the named peoples. It is not a present homeland map.
contentReviewScope: Transcript of the February 23, 1836 document on printed pages 14–15 of volume I reviewed through the Texas History Trust/University of North Texas text. The treaty’s opening and land-boundary article were inspected; the full volume, manuscript original, signatures and implementation record were not reviewed.
publicationDate: Document dated February 23, 1836; edited volume issued 1995

title: HR 1565 — Jumano Indians of Texas
annotation: The enrolled Texas House resolution documents a state legislative expression honoring the Jumano Indian Nation of Texas. Its historical narrative and population claim are not independent verification and it is not a federal recognition decision.
contentReviewScope: The enrolled resolution text was read. It is counted as a supporting primary civic record, not as a substantive historical study.

title: Atakapa Indians
annotation: A substantial Handbook of Texas synthesis useful for coastal geography, source-named groups, subsistence, trade and missions. It relies on older outsider accounts and includes dated claims about cannibalism and population decline; those claims are attributed to the article and its cited historical authors, not treated as current community facts or proof that descendants disappeared.
author: Dorothy Couser
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible Handbook entry and bibliography. Its cited books, Spanish/French records, archaeological reports and linguistic studies were not independently inspected.

title: Karankawa Indians
annotation: A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis about the coastal peoples grouped under the Karankawa name. The article is useful for chronology, named historical groups, subsistence, mobility, missions and bibliography, but carries older extinction-era framing; read it beside dated descendant accounts and do not treat its cultural-group label as a present-day government.
contentReviewScope: The full visible article body and bibliography were read. Its broad description, period terminology and claims are attributed to the TSHA entry; cited books and archival collections were not independently inspected.

title: Tonkawa Indians — Handbook of Texas Online
author: Jeffrey D. Carlisle
publicationDate: 1996; accessed through current Handbook of Texas Online page
annotation: A concise older synthesis that can be compared with the Tribe’s account, TxDOT’s 2021 report, and Jones’s 1969 study. The article includes unsourced or broad claims, dated cultural generalizations, and a 1951 statement implying the Tonkawa were no longer a distinct tribe; that last claim conflicts with the contemporary Tonkawa Tribe government and must not be repeated as a fact about present-day identity. Kept as a contextual reference, not counted toward the substantive target.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete visible article body and its “Learn More” bibliography (lines 6–47). No linked books or underlying works were read as part of this review.

title: Alabama-Coushatta Indians
author: Howard N. Martin
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
annotation: Detailed historical synthesis connecting migration, East Texas settlements, land pressures and institutions. Its sweeping cultural generalizations, assimilation framing and dated figures are not adopted here. Martin also wrote the tribe-hosted chief history: overlap is not independent corroboration.
contentReviewScope: Substantive article and bibliography, especially migration, village networks and land-policy passages; no current demographic or officer claims adopted.

title: Biloxi Indians
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
annotation: Biesele’s entry follows Biloxi families, alliances, coercive movements, and diplomacy in nineteenth-century Texas. Published in 1976 and updated in 2020. Its older terminology and conjectures about earlier migration require care; it is a regional historical overview, not a present-day community description.

title: Tigua Indians
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
author: Bill Wright
annotation: Read as an older secondary synthesis for comparison, not as a current community account. It records interpretations and population figures that differ from other published accounts and uses unqualified language-status and cultural generalizations that this profile does not adopt. Kept as a supporting reference for readers to assess its cited bibliography and dated framing.
contentReviewScope: Full online entry, introductory/history paragraphs, citations, and author-provided bibliography. Claims about present conditions, language endangerment, gender roles, membership, and legal status were not adopted as current.
countReason: Older synthesis is retained for critical comparison; its central claims require independent and community-led review before it can serve as a substantive source for this profile.

title: Domínguez de Mendoza, Juan
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online
author: Robert S. Weddle
publicationDate: Article date not stated on the accessed page
annotation: A scholarly biographical entry on Domínguez de Mendoza and the 1683–84 expedition. It describes Jumano leader Juan Sabeata’s appeal and the expedition toward La Junta, while noting disagreement over routes and the proposed San Clemente location. This is a secondary synthesis of colonial records, not the expedition diary itself.
contentReviewScope: The complete visible article and its bibliography were read. The cited expedition diary, archival manuscripts, and competing archaeological route studies were not independently inspected.

title: Jumano Indians
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online
author: Nancy P. Hickerson
publicationDate: Article date not stated on the accessed page
annotation: A substantial scholarly state-history synthesis with a bibliography. It describes several different historical groupings associated with Jumano and reviews documentary geography, trade, and migration. Its conclusion that Jumano ceased to exist as an identifiable distinct people is an interpretation of the surviving colonial record; it does not establish that descendants disappeared.
contentReviewScope: The full visible article and bibliography were read, including sections on La Junta, Tompiro communities, trade, and the article’s conclusion. The works in its bibliography and original Spanish records were not independently inspected.

title: La Junta de los Ríos
publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online
author: Bradley Folsom
annotation: A regional history of the Río Conchos–Río Grande confluence. It summarizes scholarship that treats Jumano and Patarabueye communities as either related or distinct partners, and presents a mutualistic relationship as a later interpretation. The page is useful for orientation but compresses a complex debate; its claims should be read alongside the specialist work it cites.
contentReviewScope: The full visible entry and bibliography were read, including discussion of Cabeza de Vaca, later Spanish expeditions, missions, and debated Jumano–Patarabueye relations. The cited dissertations, books, and Spanish records were not independently inspected.

title: Bird’s Fort Treaty Ratification Proclamation, 1843
publisher: Texas State Library and Archives Commission
annotation: Digitized proclamation and transcription name the Biloxi among parties to the September 29, 1843 treaty. Reviewed pp. 1–2 and the signature transcription on p. 10, identifying Hoyo Tubby. Read the complete linked document for treaty terms; the Republic’s language and diplomatic frame are historical evidence, not neutral ethnography.
authors: Republic of Texas and participating Indigenous representatives

title: 1837 Treaty between Texas and the Tonkawa — Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. I, pp. 28–29
publisher: Texas State Library and Archives Commission / Texas History Trust digital edition
author: Tonkawa head chiefs and Republic of Texas commissioner Henry W. Karnes; reproduced in the edited volume by Dorman H. Winfrey and James M. Day
type: Primary treaty text in a scholarly archival compilation
annotation: This transcribed treaty records an agreement between Tonkawa head chiefs and the Republic of Texas. Its articles describe reciprocal promises of peace and a state-appointed trading agent with a controlling role in trade. The document captures the contracting governments’ written terms and the language of its period; it does not establish how each provision worked in practice or provide a complete account of Tonkawa political decision-making. The digitized pages are part of an edited compilation of Texas Indian papers.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete treaty transcription across printed pp. 28–29 (digital pages 34–35), including the articles, signatures/marks, and ratification note. The surrounding volume is not counted as read.

title: Tribes of Texas Report
publisher: Texas Tribal Strategic Advisory Group; Texas Department of Public Safety
annotation: A 2017 public-safety broadband report includes a Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas profile and documents the Tribe’s participation in a statewide intertribal planning effort. The migration map is schematic and designed for this report’s purpose; it is not reproduced or treated as a homeland boundary. Dated population and service figures are excluded.
contentReviewScope: Inspected PDF pages 4–5, 12–13 and 19–21, including participant list, map context and Kickapoo profile; references screened. Other profiles and dated population/service figures not used.

title: History of the Northern Arapaho Tribe
publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
annotation: A substantive Northern-focused history connects changing Plains relationships, dispossession and educational institutions. The undated page is useful for historical orientation; its contemporary assessments, estimates and broad generalizations are not current measurements or substitutes for tribal accounts.
contentReviewScope: Full actual narrative read: pre-contact, nineteenth-century, early reservation and contemporary-era sections. Synthesis selects river-valley distinctions, 1878 Wind River settlement, assimilation pressures and later educational renewal.
publicationDate: Undated page; copyright and crawl dates do not establish publication

title: Language and selected grammar/learning pages — Arapaho Project collection
publisher: The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder
annotation: One learning collection offers a substantive grammar introduction alongside navigation to educational resources. Selected text explains word structure and grammatical categories. The undated landing page’s speaker estimates are excluded; linked media, dictionaries and narrative contents are not thereby inspected.
contentReviewScope: Actual language and grammar page bodies read; lesson page reviewed as navigation only. Count the related pages once. No audio listening, complete curriculum, dictionary or narrative review.

subresources.contentReviewScope: Topic list only; not inspected lesson contents.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Full explanatory body: verbs, categories, modifications, nouns and sentences.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Topic list only; not inspected lesson contents.

title: Harjo, Chitto (1846–ca. 1911)
publisher: The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Oklahoma Historical Society
author: Kenneth W. McIntosh
annotation: Read the full specialist biography. Places Harjo at Arbeka and traces his opposition to allotment, organizing, testimony, and later persecution. A concise secondary account with further-reading leads; a biography does not show unanimous community opinion, and its terminology should be read in historical context.

contentReviewScope: Main authored essay, especially Huntington's responses, oyster trade, and Reduction of Coast reservation in 1865 paragraphs. scopeClassification: Shared reservation-system context; witnesses largely concern Coos communities
contentReviewScope: Introductory scope/abridgment explanation and printed testimony excerpts, especially George W. Jackson, James Buchanan, Frank Drew and Annie Peterson. publicationDate: Memorial adopted January 2, 1907; presented to Senate January 28, 1908
annotation: This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.
contentReviewScope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. title: Pit River Tribe v. Bureau of Land Management — opinion filed September 19, 2019
publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit · National Indian Law Library transcription
annotation: Primary judicial opinion on twenty-six unproven geothermal leases at Medicine Lake Highlands. The synopsis, background, procedural history, statutory discussion, and disposition were inspected for the narrow leasing holding: one proven lease did not justify the disputed forty-year continuation of all the others. The opinion distinguishes that issue from environmental-review and trust claims; it is not a judgment restoring tribal ownership or deciding every cultural-rights question. The library provides the opinion text openly despite the introductory Westlaw citation notice.

title: The Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas: “Doing More with Less”

contentReviewScope: Entire three-page case feature read. Publication date is not stated; time-specific project descriptions were retained while dated figures were excluded.

title: Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1875, Volume II, Document 444
publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
annotation: A translated diplomatic exchange and attached Coahuila state reports concerning U.S. efforts to move Kickapoo and other Indigenous people from Mexico to U.S. reservations. It records competing U.S. and Mexican government positions, and a Coahuila commissioner’s reports of negotiations, departures, and people still at Nacimiento and elsewhere. Those documents use coercive period language and reflect government interests; their stated counts and characterizations are not treated as neutral community testimony or a complete account of consent, movement, or later residence.
contentReviewScope: Full indexed document 444 read, including the U.S. minister’s dispatch, translated Mexican foreign-ministry reply, two attached Coahuila reports, and follow-up U.S. reply. The figures and claims are attributed to the specific officials; no independent corroboration of the reported counts or agreement was established.
accessNotes: Full transcription publicly readable through the U.S. Department of State Office of the Historian.

title: Agreement with the Tonkawa Tribe for cession of lands in Oklahoma Territory — S. Ex. Doc. 52-13

type: Primary federal executive document and agreement
annotation: This federal document transmits the 1891 Tonkawa land agreement and reproduces reports from the Department of the Interior and the Cherokee Commission. It states aggregate acreage and compensation and records the commissioners’ own description of the transaction and their view of Tonkawa land rights. It is strong evidence of the government’s position and the document sent to Congress, not a neutral account of the negotiation or proof that Tonkawa participants shared the commissioners’ understanding. The individual allotment schedule and burial-location details are not reproduced in this guide.
contentReviewScope: Read the full 16-page public PDF’s transmittal, agency/commission reports, agreement articles, and selected contextual pages (PDF pages 1–6). The individualized land schedule was not reviewed in detail or reproduced; the Senate document is a government record of the agreement, not an independent account of consent or implementation.

contentReviewScope: Selected original enactment: §1(5), §2(b), Title II §§201–207, 102 Stat. 903–904 and 911–916. Independent reviewer also read the §207(e) continuation. Historical authorization, not proof of payment or conveyance; no current-law or eligibility advice.

title: Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Richards, No. 94-50369 (corrected opinion following rehearing)
author: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit; opinion by Judge Robert M. Parker
publisher: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
type: Federal appellate opinion / primary legal record
annotation: The corrected February 9, 1996 appellate opinion recounts the Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s suit over the 1866 Texas act, which provided for a one-league home site selected by the Governor. The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Texas and held that the act did not create a perfected, self-executing grant under the record and statutory language before the panel. The decision addresses that statute and case; it is not a general historical-homeland survey, a statement about present Tonkawa identity, or current legal advice. The court states that the opinion replaced its October 1995 version after rehearing to correct a factual error; only the corrected text is used here.
contentReviewScope: Read the official 20-page opinion’s opening and procedural history, its reproduction of the 1864 resolution and 1866 act, the background to the Tribe’s later claim, the statutory and Nonintercourse Act analysis, the court’s conclusion, and the rehearing correction (PDF pp. 1–5, 8–10, 12–17, 20). The underlying 1866 legislative record, district-court docket, original 1992–1994 correspondence, and later treatment of the ruling were not independently checked. Historical facts recounted by the opinion remain attributed to the court and cited sources.
publicationDate: Corrected opinion filed February 9, 1996; substituted after rehearing for the October 23, 1995 opinion

title: Patrick Anthony DeRoche — In Pursuit of the Panzacola: A Historical Documentary and Archaeological Investigation

annotation: DeRoche’s introduction explicitly places the historical Panzacola people around present-day Pensacola Bay in West Florida using seventeenth-century documentary accounts. His discussion distinguishes this people from the archaeological Pensacola culture; the test excavation did not establish a positive Panzacola site identification. Inspection: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review. Limits: The canonical name Pensacola is retained; Panzacola is the historical people-label used by the thesis. The later city and archaeological culture are separate referents. No definitive excavated Panzacola village, coordinates, ethnicity-from-ceramics inference, contemporary recognition status or disappearance claim is adopted. This is an original student thesis with committee oversight, not a statement of consensus on every historical identification.
contentReviewScope: Actual university public download, valid-TLS HTTP 200, 2,675,875 bytes, 100 PDF pages including added cover. Cover/title; abstract printed p.viii / PDF p.9; introduction printed pp.1–3 / PDF pp.10–12; and printed p.8 / PDF p.17 were read as text/OCR. Not a complete thesis or excavation-data review.
